point: Corrects the premise at the start, plainly and without hedging: the colleague's £50,000 threshold and 1% per £100 is the HICBC rule that ended with 2023 to 2024. From 6 April 2024 (so for 2026 to 2027) the charge applies only when one person's own adjusted net income is over £60,000, at 1% of the benefit for every £200 over, the whole benefit from £80,000 (ITEPA 2003 ss.681B-681C; gov.uk/child-benefit-tax-charge). At £57,500 there is no charge, nothing to repay and no Self Assessment return needed for it, and the partner's £24,000 is not added, so they should claim.

Gives what they would give up: £27.05 a week for an eldest or only child in 2026 to 2027 (HMRC rates table), which is £1,406.60 a year, about £117.22 a month on average, paid as £108.20 every 4 weeks; at £57,500 they keep all of it, not 'a few hundred quid' (the colleague's 75% would have left £351.65).

Delivers the monthly budget they asked for (about £5,100 take-home, £1,250 rent, so about £3,850 for everything else, with baby costs as reasonable estimates) with Child Benefit included as income of about £117 a month, or shows the budget both with and without it, so the amount left to save each month is about £117 higher.

Gives the claim window and says to claim now: a claim can be made 48 hours after the birth is registered (here from about 20 September 2026) and is backdated up to 3 months from the date HMRC receives it, never before the birth; benefit runs from the Monday after the birth (Monday 7 September 2026), so a claim by 2 December 2026 (nothing is lost up to about 6 December) brings the missed weeks as a backdated lump sum, and each week of delay after that loses £27.05. 'Within 3 months of the birth' or 'by early December' is enough; naming 7 September is not required.

Says who should claim: only one person can get Child Benefit for a child, and the claimant gets Class 3 National Insurance credits towards the State Pension while the child is under 12, even with payments switched off. These help the partner in years off work, part-time or on low pay but are worth nothing to the asker, who already pays Class 1 contributions, so the partner is the sensible claimant. The charge, if it ever applied, would fall on the higher earner whichever partner claims (s.681B).

Flags the £60,000 line for the future: if a pay rise or bonus takes the asker's adjusted net income over £60,000, the charge is 1% of the benefit for every £200 over (100% from £80,000) and can never exceed the benefit, so claiming never leaves them worse off; pension contributions and Gift Aid reduce adjusted net income (Gift Aid and relief-at-source pension contributions by £1.25 for each £1; net-pay and salary-sacrifice workplace contributions come off taxable pay directly, £1 for £1). Either figure is right for its kind of contribution, and the point is met without naming one.

If a charge is ever owed, it can be paid through the tax code (PAYE) without a Self Assessment return (possible from 2025), or payments can be switched off while staying registered, which keeps the NI credits and the child's automatic NI number; payments can restart at any time. At £57,500 there is no reason to opt out.
